lines.text: Now the maths. How far does it take to stop?
Draw a graph: speed up the side, time along the bottom.
The robot starts at v, its speed: four meters per second.
It brakes at a, its deceleration: six meters per second squared. It loses six meters per second, every second.
So speed falls in a straight line. The time it takes, t, is v over a. Four over six: zero point six seven seconds.
Here's the trick: on a speed-time graph, the area under the line is the distance travelled.
Two meters per second for three seconds is a rectangle: six meters. A triangle is half height times width.
Half of v, times v over a. So d, the stopping distance, equals v squared over two a.
Sixteen over twelve: one point three three meters to stop from top speed.
Now flip it. With d meters left, what's the fastest speed I can still stop from?
Solve for v: v equals the square root of two times a times d.
One meter out: three point four six meters per second. Half a meter: two point four five. At the goal: zero.
A waypoint brakes to an end speed, not zero, so the triangle becomes a trapezoid.
Then v squared equals end speed squared, plus two a d. That's the exact rule in the code.
